Read About Quito

A capital built on the shoulder of an active volcano, at an elevation that leaves visitors breathless before they've climbed a single colonial staircase.

A capital on a volcano's shoulder

Quito sits in a long, narrow valley on the eastern slopes of Pichincha, an active stratovolcano that last erupted with any real force in 1999, coating the city in ash. At 2,850 meters, Quito is either the highest or the second-highest national capital on earth — the ranking depends on which of Bolivia's two capitals you count, La Paz or Sucre — but there is no ambiguity about how the altitude feels on arrival. The air is thin enough that most visitors notice it on the first flight of stairs, and the sun at this elevation, so close to the equator, has a bite that the mild Andean temperatures don't warn you about.

The city is long and thin by necessity, hemmed in by mountains on both sides, which is why Quito has always grown the way a person grows in a narrow hallway — up, or lengthwise, rarely outward. The historic center sits in the valley's oldest, flattest ground; the newer financial district, La Carolina, occupies a plain to the north that was still countryside a century ago. Between the two, El Panecillo — a steep hill crowned with a 45-meter aluminum statue of the Virgin Mary — rises like a punctuation mark, visible from nearly everywhere in the old city.

The oldest capital in South America

People have lived in this valley for a very long time. Obsidian tools excavated on the slopes of the nearby Ilaló volcano date human presence here to roughly 8000 BC, and a settled village at Cotocollao, in what is now northwest Quito, was trading obsidian across the region by 1500 BC. The Quitu people who gave the city its name were still here when the Inca Empire, expanding north under Huayna Capac in the late 1400s, absorbed the region and made Quito the empire's northern capital.

The Spanish arrived not long after. Diego de Almagro founded a Spanish town under the name San Francisco de Quito in August 1534, but at a different location entirely — near present-day Riobamba, well south of the actual city. Quito as it stands today was refounded at its current site on 6 December 1534, by Sebastián de Belalcázar and 204 settlers, after Belalcázar's forces captured the Inca general Rumiñahui, who was executed the following January. Because of that sequence of dates, Quito is generally reckoned the oldest capital city in South America — older than Bogotá, older than Lima, older than the republics that eventually surrounded it.

The historic center is large enough to get lost in and well-preserved enough that getting lost feels like a form of time travel rather than a wrong turn.

Gold leaf and a first for UNESCO

Colonial Quito built churches with an intensity that is hard to overstate. Within decades of the city's founding, Spanish and Indigenous laborers and artisans — working under Spanish friars but drawing on pre-Hispanic techniques and a decorative instinct that was distinctly Andean — produced a body of religious architecture and art now known as the Quito School. Its signature building is the Compañía de Jesús, whose interior is sheathed almost entirely in gold leaf; its most influential institution is the San Francisco convent, begun within months of the city's founding and, at 3.5 hectares, one of the largest colonial religious complexes in the Americas.

The result of all that building is a historic center that survived largely intact into the twentieth century, in a way few other Spanish colonial capitals did. In 1978, at UNESCO's first session devoted to World Heritage, Quito's historic center was named a World Heritage Site — one of the first two ever designated, alongside the historic center of Kraków. It remains one of the largest and best-preserved historic centers in Latin America, dense with baroque facades, cobbled plazas, and working churches that still hold Mass rather than functioning purely as museums.

The line at the middle of the world

Quito is the capital city closest to the equator, which crosses the northern edge of its metropolitan area in the parish of San Antonio de Pichincha — close enough that a half-day trip from the historic center reaches it easily. The Spanish geographer who first calculated the line's precise location here did so as part of an 18th-century French scientific expedition sent to measure the shape of the earth; the monument built to mark the spot, and the small museum nearby dedicated to the Indigenous cultures who lived beside that same invisible line for centuries before anyone thought to measure it, both trade on a fact that is, when you stand there, genuinely strange to think about: half the visible ground is in one hemisphere, half in the other, and nothing about the landscape itself gives it away.

It's also the source of the city's oldest nickname, Mitad del Mundo — the Middle of the World — a phrase that shows up on everything from tourist plaques to the label on a bottle of beer, long before GPS existed to confirm it.

A city still climbing

Modern Quito keeps building on the same instinct that shaped it from the start — up, and around the mountain rather than through it. The TelefériQo cable car climbs from the city's western edge to nearly 4,000 meters on Pichincha's flank, turning a serious mountaineering approach into a twenty-minute ride with a view of the entire valley at the top. Guayasamín's Capilla del Hombre, completed after the painter's death in 1999, sits on a hillside overlooking the same valley, its murals built as a memorial to the suffering and endurance of Latin America's peoples. A new metro line, the city's first subway, opened at the end of 2023, threading beneath streets that were laid out on foot and by mule five hundred years earlier.

And an hour or two south of the city, the land keeps climbing too: Cotopaxi, one of the world's highest active volcanoes, and the páramo grassland around it, are close enough to visit in a single day and different enough from the colonial core to make the contrast the point. Quito, in the end, is a capital that never quite settled into flatness — geographically, historically, or otherwise — and that restlessness is most of what makes it worth the climb.
